definition: When a network partition occurs, a distributed data store must choose between consistency (every read sees the latest write) and availability (every request gets a response).
An extension of CAP: if there is a partition (P) choose availability or consistency, else (E) even when running normally choose between latency and consistency.
A failure that splits a cluster into groups of nodes that cannot communicate with each other although each group still runs.
A guarantee that after a write completes, every subsequent read, from any node, returns that write or a newer one.
A consistency model in which operations appear to take effect atomically at a single point between their start and end, in an order consistent with real time.
All nodes observe operations in the same single order that respects each client's own program order, though not necessarily real time.
A guarantee that operations that are causally related are seen by everyone in the same order, while unrelated operations may appear in any order.
A guarantee that if no new writes occur, all replicas will eventually converge to the same value, though reads may be stale meanwhile.
A session guarantee that a client always sees its own earlier writes, even when reading from a replica that lags.
A session guarantee that once a client has seen a value, it never later reads an older value of that data.
The minimum number of replicas that must acknowledge a read or write; with N replicas, choosing R + W greater than N makes reads overlap the latest write.
A per-node counter vector attached to data that lets a system tell whether one version happened before another or whether they are concurrent.
A logical counter that orders events consistently with causality by advancing past any timestamp it receives, without relying on wall-clock time.
A conflict-resolution rule that keeps the version with the latest timestamp and discards others; simple but can silently lose concurrent updates.
A conflict-free replicated data type whose merge operation is commutative, associative and idempotent, so replicas converge without coordination.
A technique for collaborative editing that transforms concurrent operations against each other so every client converges to the same document.
A decentralized way to spread information in which each node periodically exchanges state with a few random peers, so data reaches everyone quickly.
A background process that compares replicas and repairs differences, often using Merkle trees, so they converge.
A tree of hashes in which each node hashes its children, letting two replicas find differing data ranges by comparing only a few hashes.
Fixing stale replicas during a read: when the coordinator sees replicas disagree it writes the newest value back to the out-of-date ones.
When a replica is down, another node temporarily stores its writes with a hint and delivers them once the replica returns.
A component that suspects a node has failed, usually when heartbeats stop arriving; in asynchronous networks it can only be probabilistic.
A small periodic message sent to show that a node is alive; missing several in a row triggers suspicion of failure.
The problem of getting a group of nodes to agree on a single value or log order even when some nodes fail or messages are delayed.
A family of consensus protocols in which proposers and acceptors agree on a value through prepare and accept rounds that need a majority.
A consensus algorithm designed for understandability that elects a leader, replicates a log through it, and commits entries once a majority has them.
Choosing one node among many to coordinate work or accept writes, and choosing another when the current leader fails.
A failure state where two nodes both believe they are the leader, typically after a partition, risking conflicting writes and data corruption.
A monotonically increasing number issued with each lock or leadership grant; storage rejects requests carrying an older token, blocking stale leaders.
A lock shared by processes on different machines to ensure only one performs a critical action at a time, which needs leases and fencing to be safe.
A coordination service that offers a small, strongly consistent hierarchical store used for configuration, leader election, locks and service membership.
A strongly consistent distributed key-value store built on Raft, used for cluster configuration and coordination, notably in Kubernetes.
A protocol in which a coordinator asks all participants to prepare and then tells them to commit or abort, giving atomicity across nodes but blocking if the coordinator fails.
A long-running business transaction split into local transactions, each with a compensating action that undoes it if a later step fails.
Writing an event to an outbox table in the same database transaction as the state change, then publishing it separately so the two never diverge.
Command Query Responsibility Segregation: using separate models for writes (commands) and reads (queries), often with different stores kept in sync by events.
Storing every change as an immutable event and deriving current state by replaying them, which gives a full audit trail and time travel.
A property of an operation whose repeated execution has the same effect as executing it once, which makes retries safe.
A wrapper that stops calling a failing dependency after repeated errors, failing fast for a while and then probing to see if it has recovered.
Retrying with delays that grow geometrically (1s, 2s, 4s, ...), usually with random jitter, so struggling services are not hammered by synchronized retries.
A limit on how long to wait for a response before giving up; without timeouts a slow dependency can exhaust threads and cascade failure.
The mechanism by which services find the current network locations of one another, through a registry or DNS, as instances come and go.
An architecture of small, independently deployable services, each owning its data and communicating over the network.
An application deployed as one unit with all modules in a single codebase and process; simpler to build and test but scales and deploys as a whole.
An infrastructure layer of sidecar proxies that handles service-to-service traffic, adding retries, mutual TLS, routing and telemetry without changing application code.
A failure in which a node behaves arbitrarily or maliciously, sending conflicting information; tolerating it needs more replicas than crash-only faults.
Switching traffic or leadership to a standby component when the primary fails, ideally automatically and quickly.
